notes.text: Their strength — Bring forth as much as they are able to stand under.

The former rain — The autumn rain which is needful to mellow the earth and fit it to receive the corn. The latter rain - Needful to bring forward and ripen the fruits, accounted the latter rain because these husbandmen and vine-dressers reckoned from seed time to spring and harvest. The first month - That is, our March.
The fats — The vessels into which the liquor ran out of the press.
Wondrously — In one year giving as much as the locusts wasted in the years foregoing. Ashamed - Neither disappointed of your hopes, nor necessitated to seek relief among the heathen.
Turned — Brought the captive Israelites out of Babylon into their own land. Dream - We were so surprized and astonished.

Turn — As thou hast brought us home, bring also the rest of our brethren. As - As thou art pleased sometimes to send floods of water into dry and barren grounds, such as the southern parts of Canaan were. We must trust in God for success in all enterprizes, ver. 1, 2. And for children, ver. 3-5. A song of degrees of Solomon.

glossa.text: *A canticle of degrees.* ((CASS.)) The seventh degree, in a figure of the Old Testament, prophesies through Christ who is to come the return from captivity, as it were from Babylon: whence now consolation, and a sowing that more may be reaped. ((AUG.)) Those redeemed by the blood of Christ and turned back from captivity sing these things, while they are pilgrims, groaning by the way. Sion is Jerusalem, eternal in the angels, captive in men. *In the turning.* ((CASS.)) First the greatness of the deed is shown, with the greatness of the joy: secondly he prays for the turning from captivity still to come, there, *Turn again, O Lord. In the turning.* ((AUG.)) Or, when he shall have turned, etc., *as far as turn again, O Lord, our captivity. As.* ((ID.)) It is not always set for a likeness, but for a property, as here; whence it is also said: He did as a just man, which he truly is; so these are made *as men comforted,* that is, they rejoiced, as receiving consolation in the resurrection of Christ, who went before that we might follow.

*Our mouth.* ((CASS.)) The secret of the heart, where joys first are, which afterwards break forth by the office of the tongue. ((AUG.)) *Our mouth.* Of the heart: thence proceeds the evil and the good which cleanses or defiles us; whence not: *That which proceedeth out of the mouth, defileth ((Marc. VII))* . Not of the mouth of the flesh, but of the heart. For thou art not unclean if thou namest thefts and other evils: but while thou thinkest of them, even if thou keep silence. *Among the Gentiles.* ((ID.)) Not the Gentiles, because not all believe. *He hath magnified,* because they see them work miracles also; a firm testimony from an adversary. ((CASS.)) And he has truly magnified, lest thou doubt because of the words of the Gentiles.

*Turn again, O Lord.* ((ID.)) The second part. He prays for the turning which is to come, in which there shall be a sowing in hope of joy. ((ID.)) The redemption of the coming of the Lord having been foretold, they pray again that their own sins be forgiven. In the general remission they rejoice, and they pray pardon for themselves. *Turn again, O Lord, our captivity.* ((ID.)) There was none according to the letter in the days of David, but under the devil the world was captive, etc., *as far as* it is not therefore to be given over, because *he that soweth in tears.* ((THEOD.)) He calls Jerusalem the south, etc., *as far as* that they may be constrained, and make their way after the manner of a torrent.

*In tears.* ((AUG.)) Spiritual sowing is always in tears, whence: *Blessed are they that mourn.* But they who sow in the flesh, sow with gladness: but afterwards weeping: because *mourning taketh hold of the end of joy.* ((ID.)) Zacchaeus, *Behold the half,* etc., *as far as: He that shall give a cup of cold water shall not lose his reward ((Matth. X))*.

*Going.* ((CASS.)) By the advancement of a better life. *Casting,* sending on before them into that world. *Their own,* not of rapine, but of their own labour; *coming,* to the judgment. This is common to all, but to joy none come but the good. *And they wept.* ((AUG.)) Because they were wretched, etc., *as far as* he wishes that many be sick.

notes.text:
I exhort therefore — Seeing God is so gracious. In this chapter he gives directions,

1. With regard to public prayers

2. With regard to doctrine. Supplication is here the imploring help in time of need: prayer is any kind of offering up our desires to God. But true prayer is the vehemency of holy zeal, the ardour of divine love, arising from a calm, undisturbed soul, moved upon by the Spirit of God. Intercession is prayer for others. We may likewise give thanks for all men, in the full sense of the word, for that God "willeth all men to be saved," and Christ is the Mediator of all.

For all that are in authority — Seeing even the lowest country magistrates frequently do much good or much harm. God supports the power of magistracy for the sake of his own people, when, in the present state of men, it could not otherwise be kept up in any nation whatever. Godliness - Inward religion; the true worship of God. Honesty - A comprehensive word taking in the whole duty we owe to our neighbour.

For this — That we pray for all men. Do you ask, "Why are not more converted?" We do not pray enough. Is acceptable in the sight of God our saviour - Who has actually saved us that believe, and willeth all men to be saved. It is strange that any whom he has actually saved should doubt the universality of his grace!

Who willeth seriously all men — Not a part only, much less the smallest part. To be saved - Eternally. This is treated of, ver. 5, 6. And, in order thereto, to come - They are not compelled. To the knowledge of the truth - Which brings salvation. This is treated of, ver. 6, 7.

For — The fourth verse is proved by the fifth; the first, by the fourth. There is one God - And they who have not him, through the one Mediator, have no God. One mediator also - We could not rejoice that there is a God, were there not a mediator also; one who stands between God and men, to reconcile man to God, and to transact the whole affair of our salvation. This excludes all other mediators, as saints and angels, whom the Papists set up and idolatrously worship as such: just as the heathens of old set up many mediators, to pacify their superior gods. The man - Therefore all men are to apply to this mediator, "who gave himself for all."

Who gave himself a ransom for all — Such a ransom, the word signifies, wherein a like or equal is given; as an eye for an eye, or life for life: and this ransom, from the dignity of the person redeeming, was more than equivalent to all mankind. To be testified of in due season - Literally, in his own seasons; those chosen by his own wisdom.

glossa.text: *I beseech.* Hitherto concerning the false apostles, here concerning prayers. *First of all.* That is, that supplications be made before all things. Here the order of the Mass is shown, which is a special kind of prayer. *Supplications.* Or that prayer which is made beside or before the consecration. *Prayers.* That is, in the consecration itself. *Petitions.* Or interpellations, as it were of debt, that what is here transacted may be perfected in eternal life, as when the people is blessed by the bishop. *Thanksgivings.* Concerning things done, which conclude the whole as though the whole were from God: as, Let us bless the Lord. *For all.* That we may follow the clemency of God, because God wills all men to be saved, although according to justice he reprobates certain ones. *That quiet* from persecution.

*For this.* Lest anyone should think that these things are not to be done for those whom the Church suffers, he adds: *For this is good.* And lest anyone should think that salvation could be had by the worship of the one God and by a good life without participation in the body of Christ, that is, without the faith of the Church. *One,* he says, *God, and one mediator,* that all men be saved may never come to pass save through the mediator, God the Word, which always was, yet according to the flesh was made.

*The mediator of God,* etc. This is that arbiter whom Job desires, saying: *Would that there were an arbiter for us.* 

((AUG., lib. IX de Civit. Dei, c. 15.)) A mediator between God and men, it behoved that he should have something like to God, etc., *as far as* another good one, who reconciles enemies, Jesus Christ.

*And in truth* Truth to come is the reality and the reward of faith. Dost thou ask, the reward? let faith go before. For we believe that we may know, we do not know that we may believe. For what is faith, save to believe what thou seest not? faith therefore is, to believe what thou seest not. Truth, to see what thou hast believed.

notes.text: And if you serve God, you need be careful for nothing. Therefore take no thought — That is, be not anxiously careful. Beware of worldly cares; for these are as inconsistent with the true service of God as worldly desires. Is not the life more than meat? - And if God give the greater gift, will he deny the smaller? Luke xii, 22.
And which of you — If you are ever so careful, can even add a moment to your own life thereby? This seems to be far the most easy and natural sense of the words.
Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these — Not in garments of so pure a white. The eastern monarchs were often clothed in white robes.

The grass of the field — is a general expression, including both herbs and flowers. Into the still - This is the natural sense of the passage. For it can hardly be supposed that grass or flowers should be thrown into the oven the day after they were cut down. Neither is it the custom in the hottest countries, where they dry fastest, to heat ovens with them. If God so clothe - The word properly implies, the putting on a complete dress, that surrounds the body on all sides; and beautifully expresses that external membrane, which (like the skin in a human body) at once adorns the tender fabric of the vegetable, and guards it from the injuries of the weather. Every microscope in which a flower is viewed gives a lively comment on this text.

Therefore take not thought — How kind are these precepts! The substance of which is only this, Do thyself no harm! Let us not be so ungrateful to him, nor so injurious to ourselves, as to harass and oppress our minds with that burden of anxiety, which he has so graciously taken off. Every verse speaks at once to the understanding, and to the heart. We will not therefore indulge these unnecessary, these useless, these mischievous cares. We will not borrow the anxieties and distresses of the morrow, to aggravate those of the present day. Rather we will cheerfully repose ourselves on that heavenly Father, who knows we have need of these things; who has given us the life, which is more than meat, and the body, which is more than raiment. And thus instructed in the philosophy of our heavenly Master, we will learn a lesson of faith and cheer. fulness from every bird of the air, and every flower of the field.

Seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness — Singly aim at this, that God, reigning in your heart, may fill it with the righteousness above described. And indeed whosoever seeks this first, will soon come to seek this only.

glossa.text:
*Therefore I say to you,* etc. *Because you cannot serve God and mammon.* Be not solicitous, which is to serve riches. He has enjoined contempt of the world and confidence in things to come throughout the whole sermon, since he commanded both to bear evils and not to avenge, and to love enemies, and to flee human glory. Now he wishes to confirm it through faith in the hope of eternal things, because there are many whom the love of present things and despair of things to come make torpid.

In the sweat of the face bread is got ready, but labour is to be exercised, solicitude is to be removed, which disturbs the mind: while it fears lest either the things possessed perish or the things laboured for do not come to hand.

*Your soul.* That is, to the animal nature to which these things are necessary. Commit your whole hope to God, because you can acquire or retain nothing, except what he has decreed.

Soul is here put for life, which is sustained by food, as there: *He that loveth his soul shall lose it ((Joan. XII))*.

The animal nature is nourished by food: and is here put for life: it lives with the cattle. And he who loses it for Christ's sake shall find it spiritual unto life everlasting.

*Is not the soul?* etc. Not life for the sake of food, nor the body for the sake of raiment, but the contrary. Therefore let not the mind be solicitous, that it may receive that for whose sake it was created.

As if he should say: He who gave the greater, that is, life and body, will give also the lesser, that is, food and clothing. Let no one doubt in these promises of the truth: Let man be what he ought to be, and forthwith all things are added to him for whose sake they were made.

*Behold.* This concerning food. The saints are deservedly compared to birds, because they seek heaven, and some are so far removed from the world that they now do nothing on earth, but by contemplation alone already dwell in heaven. Of whom it is said: *Who are these that fly as clouds? ((Isa. LX))*, etc.

These examples do not forbid providence, that it should not labour, but solicitude, that your whole confidence may be in God, since even the birds live without care.

*And your Father.* He heightens and confirms the confidence of sons: because if the goodness of the Father extends itself even to those things, how much more to the sons of adoption?
*And which of you,* etc. But leave to him the care of governing the body, who made it come to this measure.

*And for raiment.* Not that this, to labour and to provide, is not fitting, but all solicitude must be cast away, and hope must be had in God. *Consider the lilies of the field.* He confirms by a sufficiently fitting example the exhortation concerning clothing.

*That not even Solomon,* etc. What purple of kings, what painting of weaving-women can be compared to flowers? The colour itself is called the covering of the flowers, as we say: a redness has covered that man.

*For if the grass of the field.* If those things which are for the use of time only, and quickly falling, shall be burnt with fire, God adorns them so beautifully.

"Tomorrow" is put for the future in the Scriptures, Jacob saying: *My justice shall hear me tomorrow ((Gen. XXX))* .

*Is cast into the oven.* Other books have: into the fire, or into a heap which has the appearance of an oven. *How much more you,* namely, will he clothe; and therefore all confidence is to be had in him; but if we are not confident even about these things, how do we hope for things invisible? Very small is the faith which is not certain even about the least things. Therefore he both presses upon us confidence about eternal things, and condemns unbelief. *Of little faith.* Whosoever doubts in any promise, is of little faith, and the more he doubts, the less he finds those things for which he was solicitous.

*Be not therefore solicitous,* etc. He more fully inculcates and turns over what he taught from the beginning of the sermon, that we should live without solicitude. *Be not,* etc. Here those seem to be reproved who, despising the common food or clothing, seek for themselves foods or garments more sumptuous or more austere than those among whom they live. *To be solicitous.* Solicitude chokes the word of God, that it may not bear fruit, and makes a man like a Gentile, that is, unbelieving.

*For all these things.* What more then has he than a Gentile: whose unbelief makes the mind anxious, and wearies it with the cares of this life? *The Gentiles.* Who have no care about things to come, but it belongs to sons to seek the kingdom. *For he knoweth.* These things are provided by God, who knows that they are necessary for us on his way. *Your Father.* Thus he makes sons secure concerning the goodness and providence of the Father, that is, without care.

*Seek therefore.* Here he plainly shows that these things are not to be sought as our goods, although they are necessary. But the kingdom of God is to be sought, and in it our end is to be placed, for whose sake we should do all things: for example: Let us eat that we may preach the Gospel, we do not preach the Gospel that we may eat. When he says "first," he signifies that this is later, not in time, but in dignity. For that is to be sought, this is necessary for the sake of that: therefore seek first the kingdom of God, that is, set it before all other things.

*And all these things.* Because all things are the sons': and therefore all these things shall be added, even to those who do not seek them, from whom if they are withdrawn, it is for a trial; if they are given, it is for thanksgiving; because all things work together unto good.

sermons.title: Upon Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount III
sermons.author: John Wesley

hymns.title: Faith, while trees are still in blossom
The Lord has done great things for us
Sheaves of summer turned golden by the sun (Una espiga dorada  por el sol)
Like a tree that's planted by the water

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)
Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Seek the peace of the city where I have caused you to be carried away captive, and pray to Yahweh for it; for in its peace you shall have peace.
echoes.note: Paul's directive to pray for kings and all in high places that believers may lead a tranquil life echoes Jeremiah's letter urging the exiles to seek the welfare of Babylon and pray to the LORD for it, because in its peace they will find peace. Both texts ground intercession for pagan rulers in the community's own well-being under foreign power. The logic of praying for the governing authority's order so that God's people may flourish is structurally identical.

echoes.text: Have I any pleasure in the death of the wicked? says the Lord Yahweh; and not rather that he should return from his way, and live?
echoes.note: God's declared desire that all be saved and come to knowledge of the truth echoes the LORD's protest that he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but desires that they turn and live. Both passages assert a universal divine will for life and salvation rather than condemnation. Verse 32 of the same chapter reinforces this with the appeal to turn and live.

echoes.text: “Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth; for I am God, and there is no other.
echoes.note: The call 'Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth, for I am God and there is no other' fuses the universal saving will with strict monotheism, precisely the pairing Paul makes in 'who desires all to be saved' and 'there is one God.' Isaiah's universal salvation offer grounded in the oneness of God stands directly behind this passage. The verbal and theological overlap is strong.

echoes.text: Hear, Israel: Yahweh is our God. Yahweh is one.
echoes.note: 'There is one God' restates the Shema's confession that the LORD is one, the foundational monotheistic creed of Israel. Paul reframes the Shema christologically by adding the one mediator, but the bedrock affirmation of divine oneness is directly drawn from Deuteronomy. This is the clearest scriptural anchor of verse 5.

echoes.text: Yet it pleased Yahweh to bruise him. He has caused him to suffer. When you make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see his seed. He shall prolong his days, and the pleasure of Yahweh shall prosper in his hand. After the suffering of his soul, he will see the light and be satisfied. My righteous servant will justify many by the knowledge of himself; and he will bear their iniquities. Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall […]
echoes.note: The Servant who makes his life an offering for sin and bears the sin of many provides the scriptural template for Christ giving himself as a ransom for all. The substitutionary self-offering 'for many' is universalized by Paul to 'for all.' The Servant Song is a primary source for the ransom theology of verse 6.

echoes.text: that they may offer sacrifices of pleasant aroma to the God of heaven, and pray for the life of the king, and of his sons.
echoes.note: The Persian decree provides for sacrifices and prayers 'for the life of the king and his sons,' a precedent for the synagogue practice of intercession for the ruling power that Paul commends to the church. This institutionalized prayer for the Gentile monarch stands behind the apostolic instruction. The continuity of Jewish intercession for kings informs the exhortation.

echoes.text: and pray for the life of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, and for the life of Baltasar his son, that their days may be as the days of heaven above the earth: and the Lord will give us strength, and lighten our eyes, and we shall live under the shadow of Nabuchodonosor king of Babylon, and under the shadow of Baltasar his son, and we shall serve them many days, and find favor in their sight.
echoes.note: Baruch directs prayer for the life of Nebuchadnezzar and his son Belshazzar, that the exiles may live under their shadow and find favor, mirroring the petition for kings so believers can live quietly. The deuterocanonical text models the very practice of interceding for a foreign sovereign's reign for the sake of the people's peace. It is a close conceptual parallel to verses 1-2.

echoes.text: Tell them, As I live, says the Lord Yahweh, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked; but that the wicked turn from his way and live: turn, turn from your evil ways; for why will you die, house of Israel?
echoes.note: The oath 'As I live, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live' restates the divine saving desire that Paul invokes in saying God wills all people to be saved. The emphatic divine self-witness to a will for repentance and life parallels Paul's theology of God our Savior. It complements the Ezekiel 18 echo.

echoes.text: There is no umpire between us, that might lay his hand on us both.
echoes.note: Job's lament that 'there is no umpire between us, who might lay his hand on us both' articulates the need for a mediator between God and man that Paul declares fulfilled in the one mediator Christ Jesus. The longing for an arbitrator standing between God and humanity is answered in verse 5. The conceptual correspondence to 'one mediator' is notable though not verbal quotation.

echoes.text: On the next day, Moses said to the people, “You have sinned a great sin. Now I will go up to Yahweh. Perhaps I shall make atonement for your sin.” Moses returned to Yahweh, and said, “Oh, this people have sinned a great sin, and have made themselves gods of gold. Yet now, if you will, forgive their sin—and if not, please blot me out of your book which you have written.”
echoes.note: Moses standing between the LORD and the people, offering himself to make atonement for their sin, typifies the role of the one mediator that Paul ascribes to Christ. The Mosaic mediation at Sinai is the paradigmatic Old Testament instance of a man interceding between God and men. Christ as mediator is read against this figural background.

echoes.text: “When you take a census of the children of Israel, according to those who are numbered among them, then each man shall give a ransom for his soul to Yahweh, when you number them; that there be no plague among them when you number them.
echoes.note: The atonement money, a ransom for each life given at the census so that no plague befall them, supplies the cultic background for Christ giving himself as 'a ransom for all.' The Hebrew kopher / lytron concept of a redemptive price for life stands behind Paul's ransom language. The universalizing 'for all' extends the Exodus ransom to all humanity.

echoes.text: The king’s heart is in Yahweh’s hand like the watercourses. He turns it wherever he desires.
echoes.note: The conviction that the king's heart is a watercourse in the LORD's hand, turned wherever he wills, undergirds the rationale for praying for rulers: God can move them toward conditions of peace. Paul's confidence that prayer for kings yields a tranquil life presupposes divine sovereignty over rulers. The link is thematic rather than verbal and is faint.

echoes.text: Don’t we all have one father? Hasn’t one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother, profaning the covenant of our fathers?
echoes.note: 'Have we not all one Father? Has not one God created us?' offers a parallel monotheistic confession linked to the unity of humanity, resonant with Paul's 'one God' grounding the universality of salvation. The pairing of divine oneness with the common bond of all people overlaps with the passage. The connection is thematic and secondary to the Shema.

echoes.text: (I stood between Yahweh and you at that time, to show you Yahweh’s word: for you were afraid because of the fire, and didn’t go up onto the mountain;) saying,
echoes.note: Moses' statement that he stood between the LORD and the people to declare the word, because they feared the fire, presents him as mediator of the covenant, prefiguring the one mediator language. The Mosaic mediatorial office informs Paul's category. The link is figural and faint.

echoes.text: none of them can by any means redeem his brother, nor give God a ransom for him. For the redemption of their life is costly, no payment is ever enough,
echoes.note: The psalm's note that no one can by any means ransom another or give to God a price for his life sets up, by contrast, the ransom that Christ alone provides 'for all.' Paul's ransom claim answers the human impossibility the psalm laments. The link is conceptual and contrastive.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Cast your burden on Yahweh, and he will sustain you. He will never allow the righteous to be moved.
echoes.note: 'Cast your burden on the LORD, and he will sustain you' — the antidote to anxiety is entrusting provision to God, the heart of 'don't be anxious for your life.'

echoes.text: I have been young, and now am old, yet I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his children begging for bread.
echoes.note: 'I have not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his children begging bread' — God's reliable provision for the righteous undergirds 'your heavenly Father feeds them... how much more you.'

echoes.text: He causes the grass to grow for the livestock, and plants for man to cultivate, that he may produce food out of the earth: wine that makes glad the heart of man, oil to make his face to shine, and bread that strengthens man’s heart.
echoes.note: God brings forth food and 'satisfies' creation — the Creator's provision for plants, beasts, and people grounds the argument from birds and lilies to human care.

echoes.text: These all wait for you, that you may give them their food in due season. You give to them; they gather. You open your hand; they are satisfied with good.
echoes.note: 'These all wait for you... you give them their food in due season' — God feeds all creatures, directly behind 'your heavenly Father feeds' the birds.

echoes.text: He provides food for the livestock, and for the young ravens when they call.
echoes.note: 'He gives to the animals their food, and to the young ravens which cry' — God feeding the birds is the precise image of 'See the birds of the sky... your heavenly Father feeds them.'

echoes.text: When the queen of Sheba had seen all the wisdom of Solomon, and the house that he had built, and the food of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their clothing, and his cup bearers, and his ascent by which he went up to Yahweh’s house; there was no more spirit in her. She said to the king, “It was a true report that I heard in my own land of your acts, and of your wisdom. However I didn’t believe the words, […]
echoes.note: Solomon's surpassing glory and splendor (the queen of Sheba's awe) is the explicit comparison: 'even Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of these' (v.29).

echoes.text: God said to him, “Because you have asked this thing, and have not asked for yourself long life, neither have asked riches for yourself, nor have asked the life of your enemies, but have asked for yourself understanding to discern justice; behold, I have done according to your word. Behold, I have given you a wise and an understanding heart; so that there has been no one like you before you, neither after you shall any arise like you. I have also given you […]
echoes.note: Solomon seeks wisdom (God's priority) and is given riches and honor 'as well' — the exact pattern of 'seek first God's Kingdom... and all these things will be added.'

echoes.text: The voice of one saying, “Cry!” One said, “What shall I cry?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, because Yahweh’s breath blows on it. Surely the people are like grass. The grass withers, the flower fades; but the word of our God stands forever.”
echoes.note: 'All flesh is grass... the grass withers' — the transience of grass that today is and tomorrow is burned (v.30) draws on Isaiah's grass-and-flower imagery of human frailty.

echoes.text: Who provides for the raven his prey, when his young ones cry to God, and wander for lack of food?
echoes.note: 'Who provides for the raven its prey, when its young ones cry?' — the divine-speech argument that God feeds wild birds, paralleling the lesson of v.26.

echoes.text: “But ask the animals, now, and they shall teach you; the birds of the sky, and they shall tell you. Or speak to the earth, and it shall teach you. The fish of the sea shall declare to you. Who doesn’t know that in all these, the hand of Yahweh has done this, in whose hand is the life of every living thing, and the breath of all mankind?
echoes.note: 'Ask the animals... the birds of the sky' — they teach that God's hand holds all life; the pedagogy of learning providence from birds matches 'See the birds of the sky.'

echoes.text: It shall be, that you shall drink of the brook. I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.” So he went and did according to Yahweh’s word; for he went and lived by the brook Cherith, that is before the Jordan. The ravens brought him bread and flesh in the morning, and bread and flesh in the evening; and he drank of the brook.
echoes.note: Ravens feed Elijah at God's command — a narrative enactment of God using birds in provision, faintly behind the birds-fed-by-the-Father motif.

echoes.text: Then Yahweh said to Moses, “Behold, I will rain bread from the sky for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day’s portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law, or not.
echoes.note: The daily manna ('a day's portion') typifies the day-at-a-time trust of 'don't be anxious for tomorrow'; Israel's wilderness schooling in non-hoarding dependence.

echoes.text: He humbled you, and allowed you to be hungry, and fed you with manna, which you didn’t know, neither did your fathers know; that he might teach you that man does not live by bread only, but man lives by every word that proceeds out of Yahweh’s mouth.
echoes.note: God let Israel hunger then fed with manna 'that he might teach you that man does not live by bread alone' — provision as a lesson in dependence, behind seeking the Kingdom first over food.

echoes.text: Commit your deeds to Yahweh, and your plans shall succeed.
echoes.note: 'Commit your works to the LORD, and your plans will be established' — entrusting one's concerns to God rather than anxious self-provision.

echoes.text: You sweep them away as they sleep. In the morning they sprout like new grass. In the morning it sprouts and springs up. By evening, it is withered and dry.
echoes.note: Humanity 'like grass which grows up. In the morning it flourishes... in the evening it is cut down' — the grass-of-the-field's day-long life behind v.30.

echoes.text: As for man, his days are like grass. As a flower of the field, so he flourishes. For the wind passes over it, and it is gone. Its place remembers it no more.
echoes.note: 'As for man, his days are like grass... the wind passes over it, and it is gone' — reinforces the perishable grass imagery applied to the field's clothing.

echoes.text: It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field. By the sweat of your face will you eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken. For you are dust, and to dust you shall return.”
echoes.note: Toil for bread and the field's produce under the curse — the labor of sowing/reaping and anxious provision that Jesus relativizes by pointing to birds that neither sow nor reap.

echoes.text: Therefore at that time also, converting itself into all forms, It ministered to your all-nourishing bounty, According to the desire of those who made supplication; That your sons, whom you loved, O Lord, might learn That it is not the growth of the earth’s fruits that nourishes a man, But that your word preserves those who trust you.
echoes.note: Manna provision teaches that 'it is not the production of crops that feeds humankind but your word that sustains those who trust in you' — Second Temple reflection on God-given sustenance versus anxious labor.

echoes.text: Envy and wrath shorten a man’s days; And care brings old age before the time.
echoes.note: 'Anxiety brings on premature old age' — Ben Sira on the harm of worry, faintly paralleling 'which of you by being anxious can add to his lifespan?'

echoes.text: Go to the ant, you sluggard. Consider her ways, and be wise; which having no chief, overseer, or ruler, provides her bread in the summer, and gathers her food in the harvest.
echoes.note: The ant gathers in summer — a nature-observation wisdom form ('consider the ant'); Jesus inverts the genre with 'consider the lilies' which do NOT toil, yet are clothed.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Do not fear, soil and seed; be glad and rejoice.
The Lord has done great things.
The threshing floors are full of grain.
The vats overflow with wine and oil.
Those who sowed in tears
come home singing, carrying the sheaves.
Come, let us worship with full hands.
The Lord has done great things for us. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Do not be afraid, O soil; be glad and rejoice, for the early rains have come and the threshing floors are heavy with grain.
The Lord has done great things for us.
Those who went out weeping, carrying the seed, are coming home with shouts of joy, their arms full of sheaves.
The Lord has done great things for us.
Look at the birds: they neither sow nor reap, and your Father feeds them. Are you not worth more than they?
The Lord has done great things for us.
So seek first the kingdom, set down your worry, and come to the harvest table with thanks.
The Lord has done great things for us, and we are glad. Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: Be glad, O soil; the rains have come.
We are filled with joy.
The barns are full, the vats overflow.
We are filled with joy.
Those who sowed in tears come home singing.
We are filled with joy.
Come, seek first the kingdom and give thanks.
The Lord has done great things for us. Amen.
